questions.q: Kevin added an index on `product.name`, yet `WHERE name LIKE '%charger%'` is as slow as before. Why?
questions.hint: In a dictionary, where would you start if you had to find every word ending in "r"?

options.text: The index is sorted by the start of the text; with a leading % it is no use
options.why: Where to look is unknown, so the database has no choice but to read every row.

options.text: The server wasn't restarted after the index was built
options.why: An index is used as soon as it is built; a restart has nothing to do with it.

options.text: Indexes don't work on Japanese text
options.why: Indexes work on text in any language. `%x%` is just as slow on English words.

options.text: Without a LIMIT, all rows have to be read
options.why: Even with a LIMIT, the rows must be read before enough matching ones can be found.

questions.q: An inverted index has laptop → 2, 5, 9 and bag → 5, 7. Searching "laptop bag", which document contains both words?
questions.hint: Look for the number that appears in both lists.

options.text: Only 5
options.why: The two posting lists overlap only at 5. Combining lists like this is the core job of a search engine.

options.text: 2, 5, 7, 9 — all of them
options.why: Each of these has at least one of the words, but only one document has both.

options.text: 2 and 9
options.why: These have only laptop and no bag.

options.text: Can't tell without reading every document
options.why: The whole point of an inverted index is to answer by combining lists, without reading documents.

questions.q: Product names were indexed with lowercase and a stemmer. Later someone swaps the query analyzer for one that keeps text exactly as typed. A customer searches "Phones". What happens?
questions.hint: Which term is stored in the index, and which term comes from the query?

options.text: Nothing matches: the index has "phone" and the search is for "Phones"
options.why: The analyzers differ, so the terms differ; a search engine matches terms exactly.

options.text: Everything works, the search engine figures it out
options.why: A search engine doesn't understand meaning. It only matches the terms the analyzer produces.

options.text: Results appear, just with a slightly lower score
options.why: If the term doesn't match at all, there is no score to lower. The result is empty.

options.text: Elasticsearch throws an error
options.why: This is a valid configuration, so no error is raised. That is why the bug is hard to spot: you silently get empty results.

questions.q: Building a brand facet with the mapping below throws an error. What is wrong?
questions.hint: A facet has to count the whole value as one exact term.

options.text: brand should be a keyword; aggregations don't work on text fields
options.why: A text field is broken into pieces by the analyzer, and aggregation is disabled on it. Counting exact values needs a keyword.

options.text: price should be text
options.why: Numeric fields are good for range filters and sorting; making it text would break both.

options.text: name has no analyzer specified
options.why: Without one, the standard analyzer runs; it has nothing to do with the brand facet.

options.text: One index can't hold two text fields
options.why: An index can have as many fields as you like.

questions.q: A customer clicks Samsung. The hits shrink to Samsung, but the brand facet now lists only "Samsung (12)" and Apple has vanished. What is the cause?
questions.hint: Was the brand condition applied before the counting, or after it?

options.text: The brand condition is in the main query, so the counts are made on Samsung products only
options.why: An aggregation counts what the query matched. In post_filter, the counts run first and the hits are trimmed afterwards.

options.text: The aggregation size is too small
options.why: size 10 allows ten brands. Only one brand was matched at all, so only one could be counted.

options.text: brand should be a text field
options.why: An aggregation on a text field throws an error; it would not quietly show one brand.

options.text: Filters are cached, so the facet is stale
options.why: The cache affects speed, not what the counts contain.

questions.q: According to BM25, in which cases does a document's score go up?
questions.hint: Remember three words: rare, repeated, short.

options.text: The matched word appears in very few documents across the whole index
options.why: A rare word carries more information, so it gets more weight (IDF).

options.text: The word appears several times inside the document
options.why: Repetition raises the score (TF), though it levels off after a point.

options.text: The document is the newest one
options.why: BM25 ignores dates. To show newer items first you need a separate sort or boost.

options.text: The match was found in a very short field
options.why: A match in short text means the text is mostly about that topic, so the score is higher.

questions.q: In which situations does it make sense to bring in Elasticsearch or OpenSearch?
questions.hint: Think about whether the problem is really there, and whether you can afford to run it.

options.text: A catalog of 3 million products; customers make typos and want facets by brand and price
options.why: The data is big, and typos and facets are exactly where database full-text is weak.

options.text: Searching 200 staff by name in an admin panel
options.why: With 200 rows, even LIKE answers instantly. A new cluster here is just extra baggage.

options.text: Hundreds of thousands of ads mixing Japanese and English, where the best-fitting ones must come first
options.why: Language analyzers and relevance scoring are what a search engine is for.

options.text: Checking whether a product is in stock at checkout
options.why: Stock decisions must be made from the database; the search index can lag behind.

questions.q: Ryan added a `search_vector` tsvector column to 500,000 products, but searches are still slow and EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan. What is missing?
questions.hint: The column holds the terms. What turns it into a word-to-rows lookup?

options.text: A GIN index on search_vector
options.why: GIN is the inverted index. Without it, PostgreSQL checks the query against every row's tsvector.

options.text: A B-tree index on name
options.why: A B-tree is sorted by the start of the text. It cannot answer "which rows contain this word".

options.text: Switching the query to LIKE '%word%'
options.why: LIKE is the slow full table scan that the tsvector column exists to replace.

options.text: Moving to Elasticsearch right away
options.why: The database route is meant for this size. One missing index does not justify running a new cluster.

questions.q: A customer searched "samsang" and got nothing back. What is the most fitting fix?
questions.hint: Search engines already have a way to tolerate a typo of one or two letters.

options.text: Turn on fuzziness in the query
options.why: Fuzziness accepts a mismatch of one or two letters and finds nearby terms.

options.text: Add every possible misspelling to the product names
options.why: There is no end to misspellings; you would pollute your data and still miss some.

options.text: Show the customer an error and ask them to spell it correctly
options.why: If they knew the right spelling, they wouldn't have misspelled it. They see an empty page and leave for another shop.

options.text: Add a stemmer filter
options.why: A stemmer unifies word forms (phones → phone); it doesn't fix spelling mistakes.

questions.q: What problems does the code below have?
questions.hint: Think separately about what happens if Elasticsearch is slow and what happens if it is completely down.

options.text: If the Elasticsearch request fails, the product stays in the database but never reaches the index, and nobody retries
options.why: This is the dual write: the first write is committed, the second is lost, and the mismatch stays.

options.text: The customer has to wait for Elasticsearch to answer
options.why: The search work sits inside the request, so if search is slow, saving a product is slow too.

options.text: flush() should have been called after writing to Elasticsearch
options.why: That makes the opposite danger: the index could hold a product that isn't in the database. And an auto-increment ID isn't available before flush anyway.

options.text: It should use POST instead of PUT
options.why: PUT with an ID is right, because it is idempotent. The problem isn't the method, it is writing to two places separately.

questions.q: In Sarah's system the message carries the new price: {id: 7, price: 500}, then {id: 7, price: 450}. Two workers finished the messages in reverse order, and the index was left with 500. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: If the message just said "look at product 7 again", would the order still matter?

options.text: Send only the ID in the message; the handler reads the latest price from the database and writes that
options.why: Then whatever order the messages run in, each run puts the database's latest price (450) in the index.

options.text: Add more workers
options.why: More workers make out-of-order completion more likely, not less.

options.text: Raise the retry count from 5 to 20
options.why: Nothing failed here. Both messages succeeded, just in the wrong order.

options.text: Add ?refresh=true to every write
options.why: Refresh controls how soon a write becomes searchable; it doesn't change which write lands last.

questions.q: A seller lists a product and goes straight to the "My products" page, but doesn't see it; 3 seconds later it appears. The page reads from the search index. What is the right fix?
questions.hint: Which place never runs behind when you want to see your own write at once?

options.text: Make the "My products" page read from the database
options.why: The database is the source of truth; reading from it lets users see their own write immediately.

options.text: Put sleep(3) in the controller after the save
options.why: Every request gets 3 seconds slower, and on a busy day the gap will exceed 3 seconds and the problem returns.

options.text: Drop the queue and write to the index straight from the controller
options.why: That brings back the dual write: if Elasticsearch fails, the product never reaches the index.

options.text: Add ?refresh=true to every index request
options.why: It doesn't shorten the wait in the queue, and forcing a refresh on every write makes indexing much slower.

questions.q: Why does IndexProductHandler stay correct even if it receives the same message twice?
questions.hint: On the second run, does anything new get created, or does the same thing just get put in place again?

options.text: The product ID is the document ID, and PUT replaces the whole document
options.why: Writing again under the same ID creates no new document; it replaces the existing one.

options.text: The handler reads the latest state from the database every time
options.why: So even on a second run, what lands in the index is correct and fresh.

options.text: A 404 from DELETE is treated as success
options.why: If the document was already removed on an earlier try, the second try gets a 404; counting that as a failure would cause pointless retries.

options.text: Messenger never delivers the same message twice
options.why: It does, for example when a worker dies after finishing the work but before acknowledging it. That is exactly why the handler must be idempotent.

questions.q: You need to change the analyzer for product names. The catalog has 2 million products, and search can't go down for even a minute. Which path is right?
questions.hint: Can you keep the old index running and build a new one beside it?

options.text: Create a new index, fill it from the database with bulk, verify it, then flip the alias
options.why: The old index serves search the whole time, and the alias moves to the new one in one atomic step.

options.text: Change the analyzer in the existing index's mapping
options.why: You can't change an existing field's analyzer; the old documents are already stored as terms under the old rules.

options.text: Delete the index and rebuild it under the same name
options.why: Until the fill finishes, search shows nothing or half the results, and that is downtime.

options.text: Restart Elasticsearch
options.why: A restart doesn't change the stored terms; an analyzer only runs at index time.

questions.q: The indexing pipeline is running. Elasticsearch went down for 2 minutes, then came back. What happened to customers saving products during that time?
questions.hint: Does the write code talk to Elasticsearch at all?

options.text: Saves succeeded as normal; the messages waited in retries, and the index caught up afterwards
options.why: The write side only touches the database and the queue. The retries (about 2, 8, 26, 80 and 242 seconds after the first failure) outlast a 2-minute outage, so no data was lost.

options.text: Every save returned a 500 error
options.why: That would happen if the controller wrote to Elasticsearch directly. In the pipeline, the write path doesn't depend on search.

options.text: Products from those 2 minutes will never appear in search
options.why: The messages weren't lost. Even once the retries run out, they sit in the failed transport and can be rerun.

options.text: The database transactions were rolled back
options.why: The database commit had already finished; a worker failure can't touch it.

questions.q: A deploy killed the PHP process right after flush() and before dispatch(). 30 saved products are missing from search and no message is in the queue. What covers this, now and in future?
questions.hint: Can Messenger retry a message that was never sent?

options.text: A nightly job that re-sends IndexProduct for products changed in the last 24 hours
options.why: It finds the products whose message was lost and re-queues them. It is safe to repeat because the handler is idempotent.

options.text: Raising max_retries
options.why: Retries only repeat a message that exists. Here no message was ever sent.

options.text: Dispatching the message before flush()
options.why: The worker could then read the database before the commit and index the old state. It also doesn't help if the process dies.

options.text: Making the handler idempotent
options.why: It already is. Idempotency makes repeats safe; it can't create a message that was never sent.

questions.q: What is wrong with the code below?
questions.hint: How many users share this one key?

options.text: The key is the same for everyone, so one user's profile will be shown to everybody for 10 minutes
options.why: The key for a per-user answer must carry the identity, such as profile.user.42.

options.text: expiresAfter(600) is too long; 60 would fix everything
options.why: A shorter expiry only shortens the leak, it doesn't stop it. The real mistake is in the key.

options.text: You can't run a database query inside the callback
options.why: You can. The callback exists to fetch from the real source on a miss.

options.text: This code won't work without Redis
options.why: CacheInterface works with any adapter; the backend isn't the problem.

questions.q: In cache-aside, in exactly what order do things happen on a miss?
questions.hint: Where does the waiter look first, and where does he go next?

options.text: Look in the cache, fetch from the database, store in the cache, answer
options.why: In this order, the next request gets its answer from the cache.

options.text: Write to the database, then look in the cache
options.why: That isn't the read order, and without looking in the cache first, the cache is pointless.

options.text: The cache fetches from the database itself and hands it to the app
options.why: That is read-through. In cache-aside the app does the fetching.

options.text: Search the database and the cache at the same time and use whichever answers first
options.why: That doesn't reduce the load on the database and defeats the purpose of the cache.

questions.q: Which data are good candidates for caching?
questions.hint: Asked again and again, heavy to build, and harmless if a little stale.

options.text: The homepage list of the top 10 products
options.why: Many people want it, the calculation is heavy, and 10 minutes old does no harm.

options.text: The category list, which doesn't change even once a day
options.why: Almost unchanging and read again and again: an ideal candidate.

options.text: The exact stock of a product at checkout
options.why: Showing stale stock leads to overselling; here accuracy matters more than speed.

options.text: A user's balance, under one key shared by everyone
options.why: Money data is harmful when stale, and under a single key one person's balance is shown to all.

questions.q: In a game app, the "like" count goes up thousands of times per second. Losing a few likes doesn't matter, but writes must be very fast. Which strategy fits best?
questions.hint: Loss is fine, but the database must be spared from every single write.

options.text: Write-behind: count in the cache and flush to the database in batches
options.why: You get speed and less database load, and losing a few likes is acceptable here.

options.text: Write-through: every like goes to both the cache and the database
options.why: Every write still reaches the database, so the load doesn't drop.

options.text: Cache-aside, deleting the cache entry on every like
options.why: Deleting thousands of times a second means there will hardly ever be a hit.

options.text: No cache, every like straight to the database
options.why: The need to absorb the load stays unsolved.

questions.q: Which statements about Symfony's get(key, callback) are true?
questions.hint: It looks like read-through, but whose code is the callback?

options.text: It is really a form of cache-aside
options.why: The callback is your app's code; the responsibility for fetching stays with the app.

options.text: The callback runs only on a miss
options.why: On a hit the stored value is returned and the slow work never runs.

options.text: You can set the expiry inside the callback with $item->expiresAfter()
options.why: Through ItemInterface you can set the expiry or tags.

options.text: The cache knows the database and runs the loader itself
options.why: The cache doesn't know the database; the callback has to say everything.

questions.q: A seller changed a product's price, but buyers kept seeing the old price for about an hour. What is the most likely cause?
questions.hint: A cache keeps a copy; who updates the copy?

options.text: The price-change code didn't invalidate the cache, and the TTL was 1 hour
options.why: The copy doesn't change with the original; it stays stale until it is invalidated or expires.

options.text: The price wasn't saved in the database
options.why: If it hadn't been saved, nobody would see the new price; here the database is right and the cache is behind.

options.text: Redis is very slow
options.why: A speed problem gives slow answers, not wrong ones.

options.text: The buyer's browser language is wrong
options.why: Language doesn't change a price's number.

questions.q: Which data should get the shortest TTL (or no caching at all)?
questions.hint: Where does a wrong value hurt the most?

options.text: A user's money balance and checkout stock
options.why: A wrong value causes direct financial loss, so here accuracy outranks speed.

options.text: The list of countries
options.why: It almost never changes; a long TTL is safe.

options.text: The top 10 products list
options.why: Being 10 minutes old harms nobody.

options.text: Old blog posts
options.why: Old posts don't change, so a long TTL is fine.

questions.q: What is wrong with the code below?
questions.hint: What gets read if another request arrives between the delete and the flush?

options.text: A request arriving between the delete and the flush can read the old value and put it back in the cache
options.why: Then the database holds the new value and the cache the old one, and nobody will delete it again.

options.text: delete() never works
options.why: It works; the problem is the order, not the method.

options.text: A cache key may not contain a dot
options.why: Dots are valid; the forbidden characters are { } ( ) / \ @ :.

options.text: changePrice() shouldn't be called before flush
options.why: Calling changePrice() before flush is correct; the flush comes after it.

questions.q: Which of these are part of designing a cache key properly?
questions.hint: What changes the answer belongs in the key.

options.text: Adding page, sort and language to a list's key
options.why: Otherwise, asking for page 2 can return the cached page 1.

options.text: Putting the user ID in the key of per-user data
options.why: This removes the risk of one person seeing another's data.

options.text: Bumping the key version when the cached shape changes
options.why: Nobody reads the old-shaped entries any more, and they die at their TTL.

options.text: Using a single key for all lists, to make it easy to remember
options.why: Different answers under one key take each other's place.

questions.q: When a product changes, three separate cache entries must go: its own page, its category list and a block on the homepage. What is the cleanest way?
questions.hint: Do you want to remember by hand where the product appears?

options.text: Give all three entries a shared tag, then call invalidateTags() once
options.why: The tag remembers that relationship, and one call deletes everything.

options.text: Empty the whole cache with cache:pool:clear
options.why: Deleting everything also throws away the hits for all other data, and the database suddenly takes a surge of load.

options.text: Set the TTL of all three to 1 second
options.why: The cache would give you almost no benefit.

options.text: Write the three keys by hand in the code and call delete()
options.why: When the product is cached in a new place, you will forget to add it here; tags protect you from that mistake.

questions.q: A category page lists 20 products. Product 42's price changes, but invalidateTags(['product_42']) leaves the old price on the list. What is missing?
questions.hint: invalidateTags() removes only entries that carry the tag.

options.text: The list entry was never tagged with product_42
options.why: Only entries carrying that tag are removed. Tag the list with each product it contains.

options.text: The TTL of the list is too long
options.why: A shorter TTL would only hide the problem; the real gap is the missing tag.

options.text: invalidateTags() works only on single-product entries
options.why: It deletes every entry with the tag, whatever its shape.

options.text: The list should have been cached with the plain CacheInterface
options.why: The plain CacheInterface has no tags at all.

questions.q: At 12 a.m., a thousand product-cache entries were all set with a 1-hour expiry. At 1 a.m. the site slows to a crawl. What is the simplest prevention?
questions.hint: Why are all the entries dying at the same moment?

options.text: Add random time (jitter) to the TTL so the entries die at different times
options.why: When the expiry is spread out, there is no storm of a thousand misses at once.

options.text: Add more memory to Redis
options.why: The problem isn't space; it is that they all die at the same time.

options.text: Raise the TTL from 1 hour to 5 hours
options.why: The storm just comes 5 hours later, and still all together.

options.text: Open more connections to the database
options.why: Running more heavy queries at once makes the database even slower.

questions.q: When the homepage cache dies, 1,000 requests go to the database together. Which solution sends just one query to the database?
questions.hint: Let one request do the job; what should the others do?

options.text: Take a lock for the key; whoever gets it rebuilds, and the rest wait or take the stale value
options.why: The heavy work runs just once at a time.

options.text: Delete the cache on every request
options.why: There would be even more misses, and the storm would get worse.

options.text: Every request runs its own query and writes to the cache, and the last one wins
options.why: That is the stampede itself; a thousand queries run.

options.text: Cut the TTL to 1 second
options.why: The entry would die more often, making even more storms.

questions.q: What is the danger in the code below?
questions.hint: What if rebuild() throws an exception or the process dies?

options.text: If the lock holder crashes, the other requests stay stuck for a long time and the PHP workers run out
options.why: The default TTL is 300 seconds, and a blocking acquire holds every worker.

options.text: Calling release() isn't actually needed
options.why: It is needed; without it the lock hangs until the TTL.

options.text: LockFactory doesn't work without Redis
options.why: Symfony Lock works with many stores (flock, Redis, database).

options.text: acquire() never returns true
options.why: It does; the problem is the endless wait.

questions.q: What are the benefits when stale-while-revalidate works properly?
questions.hint: When does the user wait?

options.text: Users almost never get a slow response
options.why: Even after the soft expiry, they get the old value immediately.

options.text: Only one request builds the new value at a time
options.why: The lock guarantees it, so the database takes no extra load.

options.text: The cache never shows a value even a few seconds old
options.why: On the contrary: the price of this technique is showing a slightly old value for a while.

options.text: It is the best approach for an account balance
options.why: A stale value is not acceptable for a balance; avoid caching it altogether.

questions.q: Which is true about Symfony's get($key, $cb, beta: 1.0)?
questions.hint: When does beta act, and for whom?

options.text: Shortly before the expiry, some request may, with a small probability, rebuild the value early
options.why: This is probabilistic early expiration; it avoids a storm at the moment of expiry.

options.text: Setting beta: 0 turns this early renewal off
options.why: beta 0 means no early renewal; a miss happens only once the entry has expired.

options.text: beta decides how many years the data stays in the cache
options.why: expiresAfter() sets the lifetime; beta is only the tendency toward early renewal.

options.text: Symfony cache doesn't work without beta
options.why: beta is optional; the default is 1.0.

questions.q: What does the header below mean?
questions.hint: The browser and the CDN get different lifetimes.

options.text: The browser may keep it for 60 seconds and the CDN for 600; after expiry, a copy up to 120 seconds old may be used
options.why: s-maxage is for shared caches only, max-age is for the browser; SWR permits the old copy.

options.text: No cache will keep anything
options.why: That is what no-store means.

options.text: Only the user's browser will keep it, for 600 seconds
options.why: public says the CDN may keep it too, and 600 is the s-maxage, which is the CDN's.

options.text: It must ask the server every time
options.why: That is no-cache; here there is no need to ask within the lifetime.

questions.q: A client holds the ETag "v7a1". The product hasn't changed on the server. What happens when the client sends a request with If-None-Match?
questions.hint: It hasn't changed, so is there any need to send the body?

options.text: The server replies 304 Not Modified with no body, and the client uses its own copy
options.why: The fingerprint matches, so the download is saved.

options.text: The server replies 200 and sends the whole body again
options.why: That happens when the fingerprint doesn't match, meaning the product has changed.

options.text: The server replies 404
options.why: 404 means the resource doesn't exist; here it exists, it just hasn't changed.

options.text: The client sends no request at all
options.why: It does, to validate after the lifetime ends. Sending no request is max-age's job.

questions.q: On which answers is it safe to put Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=600?
questions.hint: Is it the same for everyone?

options.text: A product list that is the same for everyone and holds no personal data
options.why: Every user gets the same answer, so the CDN's copy is correct for all.

options.text: A hashed app-3f9a1c.js
options.why: When the contents change, the name changes, so the copy never goes stale.

options.text: A logged-in user's cart
options.why: It differs per user; the CDN would show the first person's cart to everyone.

options.text: /api/me, reached with an Authorization header
options.why: A personal answer; making it public leaks data.

questions.q: After a new deploy, Ryan says, "Some users still see the old JS." app.js has a max-age of 1 year and no hash in its name. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: How would a browser know the file has changed?

options.text: Add a hash of the contents to the file name (app-<hash>.js) and link the new name in the HTML
options.why: A new name is a new URL and so a new cache key; the old copy has no effect.

options.text: Set the max-age to 5 seconds
options.why: It kills the benefit of caching; the file would be downloaded every time.

options.text: Ask users to press Ctrl+F5
options.why: Putting the burden on users is not a fix.

options.text: Use no-store
options.why: Then 2.4MB would be downloaded every time, creating waste right where the problem is.

questions.q: Ryan hashes his JS file names and gives them a one-year lifetime, but also gives the HTML page max-age=1 year. After a deploy, what do returning users get?
questions.hint: Where do the links to the new hashed names live?

options.text: The old HTML from their cache, which still links to the old JS file
options.why: The new names appear only in the new HTML, which the browser never fetches while its copy is fresh.

options.text: The new JS file, because its name is new
options.why: The browser only asks for a new name if it reads new HTML that mentions it.

options.text: An error, because the old file was deleted
options.why: The old file is still served, which is why it keeps working, just outdated.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the hash protects the HTML too
options.why: The hash is in the JS name only; the HTML keeps the same URL, so it needs a short lifetime or no-cache.

questions.q: What is wrong with the Symfony code below?
questions.hint: Who is the CDN keeping a copy for?

options.text: With public and smaxage, the CDN can show one user's orders to others
options.why: The answer depends on getUser(), but the CDN's key is just the URL.

options.text: The smaxage value is too large; 30 seconds would be safe
options.why: The leak happens with a short lifetime too, just for less time.

options.text: You can't put cache headers on a JsonResponse
options.why: You can; they go on every Response.

options.text: There is no problem, because Symfony handles everything itself
options.why: When you write public explicitly, Symfony obeys; the responsibility is yours.
